ch09 - Hello, My Name is Inigo Montoya. You Bought This Book. Prepare to Enjoy!.md
chapters.relation: The collection's introduction, written as a parody of the movie's bedtime-story frame: a man claiming to be both the sixteenth Dread Pirate Roberts and a descendant of S. Morgenstern tells the editors how the adventures of the Man in Black, Inigo, Fezzik, Buttercup, Prince Humperdinck, and Miracle Max teach lessons in logic, metaphysics, ethics, philosophy of language, and political philosophy. It repeats Vizzini's boast that Plato, Aristotle, and Socrates were morons (whom the philosophers 'weren't buying') and jokes that everything is 'inconceivable!' - 'I do not think it means what he thinks it means' - before closing with 'As you wish!'

chapters.file: ch10 - Part I Deceptive Words.md
ch11 - 1. True Love and False Fronts.md
chapters.relation: Fallis argues the movie is really about lying and duplicity, not true love: Humperdinck frames Guilder for Buttercup's abduction, the Dread Pirate Roberts is a serial persona, and even the heroes bluff their way into the castle. He treats this as 'adversarial epistemology,' showing that Descartes's malicious demon and Kant's argument that universalized lying is impossible only rule out extreme scenarios and cannot unmask mundane deceivers like Vizzini and Humperdinck (a point he sharpens with Parfit's objection that liars sometimes profitably tell the truth). What does real work are Hume's tools for evaluating testimony: Valerie catches Miracle Max lying about 'to blave' by asking what he has to gain, and Buttercup catches Humperdinck when his claim that every ship in the armada will accompany the honeymoon contradicts his promise of the four fastest ships.

chapters.file: ch12 - 2. Why Men of Action Don’t Lie.md
chapters.relation: Mahon maps the film's non-romantic relationships onto Aristotle's philia: the loyal friendship of Inigo and Fezzik under Vizzini's abuse, expanded into a four-person 'family' once Westley, who defeated and spared them with respect, joins them to storm the castle. He argues deception in the film tracks the absence of philia - bad men incapable of friendship (Vizzini, Humperdinck, Rugen) lie to anyone, while friends never lie to each other and the early duels are sportsmanlike. Westley's line 'We are men of action. Lies do not become us' encodes an honor code that real men do not lie to real men even when enemies (hence Westley cheats Vizzini in the Battle of Wits with both goblets poisoned, and the chapter analyzes the resulting triple- and quadruple-bluff regress), while the one exception - Westley letting Buttercup stay deceived about Humperdinck - exposes the code's chauvinism, matching Aristotle's view that philia in its purest form exists only between male equals.

chapters.file: ch13 - 3. The Magic of a Promise.md
chapters.relation: Alloy reads the whole story as being about promises - Westley's 'I will always come for you,' Humperdinck's insincerely made and casually broken vows to Buttercup, and Inigo's vow of vengeance to his murdered father. He tests conventionalism, using Rawls's idea that breaking a promise cheats on a fair rule-bound practice (illustrated by Inigo's rule-governed duel and the Battle of Wits where both parties cheat), against expectationalism, on which obligation comes from the trust and expectations created, as when Humperdinck manipulates Buttercup through her trust. Both theories struggle with Inigo's promise to a dead man, so Alloy argues with Searle that it is responsibility for intent that makes a promise, and defends his own view - against the Hobbesian consensus - that every promise is also a self-promise whose binding force is the promisor's self-respect: promises 'make us people.'

chapters.file: ch14 - 4. That Moron Aristotle on the Means of Persuasion.md
chapters.relation: Wolfe applies Aristotle's definition of rhetoric - seeing the available means of persuasion, where success depends on the speaker's character, the audience's emotional state, and the argument's content - to show that Westley is the story's master rhetorician while Humperdinck is a poor one. Humperdinck fails by coasting on his title ('I am your Prince and you will marry me'), whereas Westley plays on Inigo's mind during the cliff climb, demoralizes him with the left-handed switch, neutralizes Fezzik's strength with a chokehold, exploits Vizzini's overconfidence in the Battle of Wits, and reverses the 'to the pain' situation by targeting Humperdinck's cowardice and vanity. The chapter also sets Aristotle's neutral view of rhetoric against Socrates's suspicion of it as sophistry (relented from in the Phaedrus).

chapters.file: ch15 - 5. Does It Mean What Vizzini Thinks It Means.md
chapters.relation: Fetterman takes Inigo's 'I do not think it means what you think it means' seriously and defends Vizzini: the line may merely record that two speakers define 'inconceivable' differently, or react to it differently. Using Wittgenstein, he argues communication requires agreement in judgments, so Vizzini and Inigo may simply be playing different language games, like users of two different dictionaries. He then runs Wittgenstein's private language argument against the possibility that Vizzini's usage is correct by his own idiosyncratic rules - a purely private definition could never be confirmed or be wrong, since only Vizzini checks it - and touches on the philosophical sense of 'conceivable' as logically possible (the square circle) and the group language game that lets everyone accept Miracle Max's 'to blave.'

chapters.file: ch16 - Part II Courage and Reason.md
ch17 - 6. To the Pain.md
chapters.relation: Robison-Greene imagines the table of contents of Count Rugen's definitive book on pain, using the Zoo of Death and The Machine as her case studies. Bentham's dimensions of pain - intensity, duration, and propinquity - organize the analysis of Westley's torture, including Rugen's tactic of leaving The Machine beside the prisoner so anticipation itself hurts, and the metaphysical oddity of having years stolen from the far end of one's life. Mill's higher and lower pleasures explain why the orangutan's prolonged death disturbs us more than other kills (a chimpanzee can reflect on what is happening to her), and Singer's speciesism grounds the argument that animals' pain behavior shows they suffer, so inflicting it merely because they are animals is indefensible; by contrast Westley's empathy lets him out-sadist the sadists with the 'to the pain' speech.

chapters.file: ch18 - 7. Who Should Have Won the Battle of Wits.md
chapters.relation: Greene observes that the Battle of Wits never really happened - Westley implied the iocane was in one goblet but poisoned both - so he constructs a 'near possible world' (crediting David Lewis's realist take on possible worlds) in which a fair contest occurs between the same two men. Vizzini's verbal 'deduction' is specious, he is hopeless at reading people (every 'inconceivable!' marks an underestimate), and his hubris and compulsive trickery make him predictable, while Westley reads character expertly, from Inigo's oath on his father's soul to Fezzik's sportsmanship. Greene concludes that in the majority of possible worlds the Man in Black wins a fair battle, and cheated in ours only because his real goals were getting the knife from Buttercup's throat and seeing Vizzini dead.

chapters.file: ch19 - 8. I Will Never Doubt Again.md
chapters.relation: Watson and Guidry-Grimes ask whether Buttercup was rational to accept the evidence that Westley was dead, and whether Westley's Fire Swamp optimism and Inigo's twenty-year hunt for the six-fingered man are wishful thinking or something better. After laying out the evidentialist tradition (Descartes's rule of evidence, Hume's 'a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence,' Clifford's condemnations), they use Adrienne Martin's account of hope as 'endorsed desire plus uncertainty' to argue that value-shaped belief can be rational when it sustains well-being and character. Their conclusion expands rationality beyond evidence-tracking: hope, unlike wishful thinking, takes evidence seriously while balancing it against what makes a life good, which is why Buttercup's despair on the wedding night, not her earlier resignation, is the real failure.

chapters.file: ch20 - Part III Getting Even.md
ch21 - 9. Why Revenge Is So Sweet.md
chapters.relation: Haas asks why we cheer Inigo's vendetta against Rugen when moral philosophy condemns vengeance as emotionally driven injustice. Distinguishing impartial, proportional punishment from personal revenge, he then uses the honor-culture literature (Nisbett and Cohen, Tamler Sommers) to argue that in lawless Florin - where the 'justice system' is run by the villain who ordered the murder - Inigo's personal retribution is a justified duty of honor, since no institutional avenue exists. The deeper pull of revenge stories, he concludes, is that victims have a special moral standing to punish - which is why Rugen dying by anyone's hand but Inigo's would be unsatisfying - while a variant story (Westley as the killer) would call instead for atonement and forgiveness, showing that revenge is made admirable by how stories are told.

chapters.file: ch22 - 10. Making the Punishment Fit the Crime.md
chapters.relation: Heter defends Inigo's killing of Rugen as pure retribution - not deterrence or prevention, since Rugen 'deserves' to die for a murder long past. Locke's state of nature grounds the right to punish in victims, who merely transfer it to the state for prudential reasons, so in tyrannical Florin, where no reasonable expectation of justice exists, Montoya is within his rights to execute punishment himself. Kant's retributivism (the island whose inhabitants become accomplices if they spare convicted murderers, from the Metaphysics of Morals) supports the claim that murderers deserve death, and against the objection that proportionality need not mean identity of kind (following M.A. Moore, using Fezzik's hypothetical house-burning), the chapter argues death is the only punishment weighty enough to fit murder.

chapters.file: ch23 - 11. Have Fun Overthrowing This Evil Government!.md
chapters.relation: Gibson reads Humperdinck's fabricated-pretext war against Guilder (framing Guilder for Buttercup's murder, with Vizzini's crew as private military contractors) through Just War Theory: it fails the jus ad bellum just-cause requirement built on Augustine and Aquinas, since the war would be retribution sparked by staged wrongdoing, and contractor motives of profit compound the violation. Michael Davis's critique of the ticking-time-bomb defense then shows that Rugen's torture of Westley is exactly the 'institution of torture' whose moral cost forbids ever licensing torture, since the torturer must be trained on victims first. Finally, even Hobbes's Leviathan - the most absolutist of social contract views - requires the sovereign to protect the people's safety and administer equal justice, so Humperdinck's record makes his rule illegitimate and the storming of the castle a justified insurrection.

chapters.file: ch24 - 12. Should I Really Stop That Rhyming.md
chapters.relation: Yuen uses the rhyming scene to analyze annoyance - rhyme hijacks Vizzini's attention, the Goldman/Morgenstern interruptions betray invested expectations, and fans' endless quotation is annoying through sheer repetition - concluding that annoyance is irreducibly relative and contextual. Aristotle's virtue theory supplies the moral frame: friendliness and wittiness, golden means between obsequiousness and surliness, buffoonery and boorishness, make being annoying a character flaw that damages the communal eudaimonia Aristotle takes the good life to require. Since these virtues may be supererogatory ideals rather than obligations, Yuen borrows Kant's imperfect duty to develop one's talents to explain why Inigo had to become a master swordsman - failing to hone the skill his one great goal demands would be a failure of self-respect.

holes.name: The Obligation of Promises
holes.what: The philosophical question of how promises create obligations, debated between conventionalist accounts (Rawls), expectationalist accounts, and self-respect based accounts (with Searle and Scanlon as key reference points).
holes.why: Chapter 13 is entirely about what makes promises binding - Westley's 'I will always come for you,' Humperdinck's broken vows, and Inigo's vow to his dead father - and the taxonomy has no concept covering promising.

holes.name: Rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Rhetoric of persuasion as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in each case, via the speaker's character (ethos), the audience's emotional state (pathos), and the argument itself (logos).
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire framework is Aristotle's Rhetoric applied to Westley's victories and Humperdinck's failures, but the taxonomy has no rhetoric concept for Aristotle.

holes.name: Evidentialism (Clifford's rule)
holes.what: The view that belief is rational only when proportioned to evidence, crystallized in W.K. Clifford's 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.'
holes.why: Chapter 19 sets this evidentialist tradition (Descartes, Hume, Clifford) against hope-driven belief, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for the evidence-only side of the debate.

holes.name: Honor Cultures
holes.what: The Nisbett-Cohen-Sommers distinction between lawless honor cultures, where personal retaliation for attacks on one's honor is a rational duty, and institutionalized cultures with state-administered justice.
holes.why: Chapter 21's defense of Inigo's revenge turns on Florin being an honor culture with no functional justice system, a framework the taxonomy does not cover.

holes.name: Supererogation (acts beyond duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally praiseworthy and encouraged but not required, going above and beyond the call of duty.
holes.why: Chapter 24 proposes that Aristotle's virtues of friendliness and wittiness are supererogatory ideals rather than obligations, using supererogation as a load-bearing concept the taxonomy lacks.
